# Branch Naming
Engineering branches use the format `type/short-description`, for example `feature/profile-search` or `fix/login-timeout`.
# Pull Request Submission

Push your branch to the company Git repository and open a pull request against the `main` branch. Include a clear summary, testing notes, and screenshots when the change affects the UI.
# Reviewer Requirements
Every production-bound pull request requires at least one reviewer from the owning engineering team. Changes affecting security or data access require an additional reviewer familiar with the affected area.

# Approval and Merge
Address reviewer comments before merging. A pull request may be merged after required approvals and successful CI checks. The author should use squash merge unless the team manager documents another strategy.

# Eligible Expenses
Reasonable business travel, approved client meals, and pre-approved work expenses may be reimbursed when supported by receipts.
# Reimbursement Process

Submit the expense through the company expense portal. Select the appropriate category, attach the receipt, and add a short business purpose.
# Submission Deadline
Expenses should be submitted within 15 calendar days after the expense date.

# Required Receipts
Receipts are required for reimbursable expenses. If a receipt is unavailable, contact Finance before submitting the claim.

# First Day Arrival
New employees should arrive at the Vijayawada office by 9:30 AM on their first day. Reception will issue a temporary visitor badge.
# WiFi and IT Support

Connect to the company network named Company-Guest on day one. For IT issues, open a ticket through the internal IT Help Desk and include your device name and a short description.
# First-Day Checklist
Complete HR onboarding, activate company email, collect your employee badge, attend the office tour, and meet your manager.

# Office Tour
The office tour covers reception, meeting rooms, engineering workspace, pantry, and the emergency assembly point.

# Departments
The company has Engineering, Design, Sales, Finance, People Operations, and Customer Success departments.
# Engineering Team

Engineering owns product development, reliability, internal tooling, and technical quality.
# Engineering Manager
The Engineering Manager coordinates engineering priorities, team rituals, and onboarding support.

# Team Responsibilities
Product teams work cross-functionally with design and sales. Engineers participate in standups, reviews, planning, and incident response as relevant to their team.

# Remote Work Rules
Employees may work remotely on approved days according to their team arrangement. Keep your calendar and working location current.
# Meeting Expectations

Join scheduled meetings on time, keep your status current, and communicate early when you cannot attend.
# Communication Guidelines
Use company chat for quick coordination, the issue tracker for work items, and documented channels for decisions that teammates may need later.

SECTION 01
The short version
If you read nothing else, read these six lines.

WHAT ACTUALLY WINS THIS
Not the prettiest UI — polish is 20 points out of 100. 65 points sit on shipping what you promised, structuring your code
sensibly, and being able to explain and modify it. A modest app that is finished, robust and understood beats an
ambitious app that is half-built and unexplained. Every single time.

You are judged against your own Scope Card, which you submit in the first 45 minutes. Promise three screens and
deliver three polished screens, and you beat a team that promised ten and delivered six broken ones. Scope small.
Finish it. Then extend.
1

Your deployed URL is the submission. Not localhost. Not a laptop. If the URL does not load at 14:30, you score zero
on the largest criterion.
2
A judge will resize your site to 375 px wide. Every team, every time. Build mobile-first or you will lose these marks.

3
A judge will spend sixty seconds actively trying to break your app. The exact list of what they will do is printed on
page 4. There are no surprises — use it as a checklist.
4

AI tools are fully allowed. No marks are deducted for using them. But a randomly chosen team member will be asked
to explain a file and make a live change to it.
5
Empty states, loading states and error messages carry real weight. They are the fastest marks available and almost

every team forgets them.
6
2
Your Scope Card — due 09:45, then locked

Seventy-five words maximum, submitted through the form. Once locked, it does not change. Judges score your delivery
against it.
ProblemOne sentence. What is broken and for whom.
Target userOne line. Be specific — "second-year students booking lab slots", not "everyone".

Core featuresThree to five, that must work by 14:30. This is what you are graded on.
Stretch featuresTwo. Only these count toward a top score on scope delivery.
Data sourceWhich option from page 6 you are using.
THE MOST COMMON WAY TEAMS LOSE

Declaring eight core features at 09:45 because it sounds impressive, then delivering four of them badly. Judges see the
card. Ambition on paper that you do not ship costs you marks — it does not earn them.
SECTION 02  ·  SCREENING ROUND
How Round 1 is scored

Every team is judged by a pod of two judges: 4 minutes to demo, 2 minutes of questions. Three criteria,
0–4 each. The top teams from each pod go to the finals.
C1   Does your declared core flow work
0

Blank screen, build error, or the URL is dead.
1
Page loads, but the core flow breaks partway through.
2

Core flow completes end to end, with visible bugs along the way.
3
Core flow plus at least one secondary declared feature work cleanly.
4

Everything on your Scope Card works. No bugs found in four minutes.
C2   UI craft and responsiveness
0
Unstyled or genuinely unreadable.

1
Styled, but inconsistent spacing and type. Breaks badly at mobile width.
2
Clean but generic — a template or default AI output, left unmodified.

3
Consistent spacing and type scale, clear hierarchy, works at 375 px.
4
All of the above, plus deliberate decisions: considered colour, hover and focus states on interactive elements, no layout

shift.
3
C3   Does it survive the stress test
0

Crashes or white-screens on the first thing tried.
1
Survives a refresh but breaks on bad input.
2

Handles bad input, but all your state resets on refresh.
3
State persists, empty and loading states present, nothing crashes.
4

All of the above, plus real error handling — a failed request shows a message, not a frozen spinner.
READ THE 2S CAREFULLY
Notice that "clean but generic, unmodified template output" is a 2 out of 4, not a 3. A good-looking default is exactly
what everyone will arrive with. The marks are in what you changed and why you changed it — be ready to say so.

SECTION 03
The stress test — published in full
A judge will do these seven things to your app, in this order, while you watch. Run them on yourself at
13:00 and fix what breaks. This is the single best use of an hour you will find today.

WHAT THE JUDGE DOESWHAT YOU NEED TO HAVE BUILT
1Resizes to 375 px wide.Layout reflows. No horizontal scroll, no overlapping text,
navigation still usable.
2Refreshes mid-flow — halfway through your main

task, hits reload.
State survives via localStorage or URL params, or falls back
gracefully to a sensible start.
3Submits an empty form.An inline validation message. Not a crash. Not silence.

4Pastes 400 characters into a short text field.Truncate, wrap, or reject. Your layout must not explode.
5Double-clicks submit rapidly.Button disables while working, or duplicates are prevented.
6Searches for something that does not exist.An empty state with a message. Not a blank white area.
7Goes offline and triggers a request.An error message. Not an infinite spinner.

WHY THIS EXISTS
Empty states, loading states, error handling and input validation are the parts of frontend work that get skipped under
time pressure, and that generative tools do not produce unless you specifically ask. They are cheap to add and they are
worth 15–20% of your score. Budget forty minutes for them.

SECTION 05
The AI policy

You may use any AI tool. ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, Cursor, v0, Lovable, Bolt — all permitted. No marks are
deducted for using them.
Two conditions. First, list every tool you used in your README. Second, be able to explain and modify any code you
submit.

The code-ownership check
In Round 1 a judge picks one team member at random — not the presenter — and asks them to open a file and explain it. In
the finals this becomes a full 20-point criterion with a live task: three minutes, your machine, judges watching.

USING AI DURING THE LIVE TASK IS FINE
Using an assistant fluently to make a change you clearly understand scores a 2 or 3. Pasting the whole file in and hoping
scores a 0. The difference is whether you know where the change goes before you ask for help. So: whatever you

generate today, read it. Ten minutes spent understanding your own state logic is worth more than another feature.
NON-DISCLOSURE IS THE ONLY VIOLATION
Heavy AI use, declared honestly, costs you nothing. Heavy AI use, undeclared, is grounds for disqualification. Just write
the list in your README.

Hackathon Problem Briefs: AI Onboarding Assistant for New Employees 
1. Problem Context 
New employees ask repetitive onboarding questions—where are the office keys, what's our code 
review process, how do I submit a reimbursement claim? HR and managers answer the same

questions dozens of times. Existing knowledge often lives scattered in Slack threads, Google 
Docs, outdated wikis, or someone's head. Without a centralized, searchable, AI-powered 
resource, ramp-up takes longer and consistency suffers. Companies can't scale onboarding 
without hiring more HR staff or creating rigid, impersonal flowcharts.

2. Objective 
Build a web app where admins upload company docs, policies, and org structure, and new 
hires ask a conversational AI assistant grounded in those documents for onboarding help. The 
AI should also auto-generate a personalized first-week checklist by role and flag questions

that need human escalation (HR/manager). Include an admin dashboard showing common 
questions to identify documentation gaps. 
3. Core Features (Must-Have) 
• Admin document upload: File upload interface (PDF, Markdown, plain text) for

company docs—onboarding guides, policies, team structure, process docs. Store them 
with metadata (title, category, upload date). 
• Document ingestion & indexing: Parse uploaded docs and store embeddings or chunks 
in a vector database (for semantic search) or simple full-text search.

• Conversational AI assistant: Chat interface where new hires ask questions in natural 
language. AI responds with answers grounded in uploaded docs, with citations showing 
which doc/section it used. 
• Escalation detection: AI flags questions it can't answer with high confidence (e.g.,

"When will I get my bonus?") and routes to HR/manager queue. 
• Role-based checklist generation: New hire selects their role (Engineer, Designer, Sales) 
during onboarding. AI generates a personalized first-week checklist pulling from docs 
(e.g., "Set up GitHub access," "Attend team sync," "Review code guidelines").

• Admin dashboard: Shows a list of common questions new hires ask, which can help 
leadership identify missing documentation. 
• New hire profile: Store hire name, start date, role, and chat history for admins to 
reference.

4. Stretch Features (Good-to-Have) 
• Multi-language support: Auto-translate assistant responses and docs for global teams. 
• Feedback loop: New hires rate assistant responses (thumbs up/down); admins see low-
rated QA pairs to improve docs.

• Document version control: Track doc updates; admins can see which docs changed and 
re-index them. 
• Slack integration: Deploy the assistant as a Slack bot so new hires don't leave their chat 
app.

• Pre-boarding flow: Send onboarding questions to incoming hires before day 1; admins 
see them in advance. 
5. Suggested Tech Stack 
• Frontend: React – multi-step onboarding flow (role selection, checklist view, chat

interface). 
• Backend: Node.js + Express or Python + Flask – handles doc uploads, 
embedding/indexing, and AI assistant API calls. 
• Vector database / search: Pinecone (free tier, no DevOps) or Supabase + pgvector

(PostgreSQL with vector extension). For MVP, even simple TFIDF  full-text search with 
MongoDB is fine. 
• LLM/AI: OpenAI API (GPT-3.5 or 4) or open-source Llama via Hugging Face API. 
Write prompts that include "Answer only using the provided documents..." to ground

responses. 
• Document storage: Firebase Storage or AWS S3 free tier (or just store raw text in 
database for MVP). 
• Database: Firebase Firestore or MongoDB Atlas – store docs, user profiles, chat history,

escalated questions. 
• Hosting: Vercel + Railway or similar. 
Why? Pinecone handles vector search with minimal setup; OpenAI's API is reliable and fast for 
grounded QA. If budget is tight, full-text search + simple keyword matching works for MVP.

6. Suggested Approach / Step-by-Step Plan 
1. Set up backend & frontend scaffolds (30 min): Node + Express + React boilerplate, 
GitHub repo. 
2. Design data models (30 min): Schema for documents (title, content, category,

upload_date), new hire profiles (name, role, start_date), questions (text, asker_id, 
timestamp, escalated), and chat history. 
3. Build admin upload & doc management (1.5 hrs): React component for file upload, 
backend endpoint /upload-doc that parses and stores docs in database. Start with

simple text storage (no embeddings yet). 
4. Implement document search/retrieval (1.5 hrs): Add a search function that finds 
relevant docs when AI needs context. Use TFIDF or basic keyword matching for MVP. 
5. Build new hire onboarding flow (1.5 hrs): React multi-step form: role selection →

checklist generation → chat interface. Mock the checklist for now. 
6. Integrate OpenAI API for chat (1.5 hrs): Write a backend endpoint /ask that takes a 
question, retrieves relevant docs, and uses GPT to generate a grounded answer. Include a 
prompt like: "Using only the provided company documents, answer this question:

[question]. If you can't answer, say so." 
7. Implement escalation logic (1 hr): After AI generates an answer, check confidence 
score; if below threshold (hardcode 0.6 for MVP), flag for escalation. Add escalated Q 
queue visible to admins.

8. Build admin dashboard (1.5 hrs): Simple page showing common questions, escalated Q 
queue, and list of uploaded docs with stats. 
9. Polish & test (1.5 hrs): End-to-end testing (admin uploads docs → new hire asks 
questions → AI answers + escalates appropriately), handle edge cases (empty docs, API

failures). 
10. Demo preparation (30 min): Pre-populate with sample company docs (mock HR 
policies, team structure) so demo runs smoothly. 
Total: ~12 hours – leaves room for refinement and stretch goals.

7. Sample Data / APIs to Use 
• Mock company documents: Create sample docs (Markdown/text files):  
o "Onboarding Guide.md" – overview, first day checklist, office tour 
o "Engineering Code Review Process.md" – PR guidelines, tools, approval steps

o "Expense Reimbursement Policy.md" – what's covered, submission process, 
deadlines 
o "Team Structure.md" – org chart, manager names, department descriptions 
o "Work From Home Policy.md" – remote work guidelines, meeting norms

• Sample new hire questions (to test the assistant):  
o "Where's the office and what time should I arrive on day 1?" 
o "How do I submit a code review?" 
o "What's the process for expensing a conference ticket?"

o "Who's my manager and what's the engineering team structure?" 
• OpenAI API: Free tier is plenty for ~50 conversations during the hackathon. 
8. Key Challenges to Anticipate 
• Grounding accuracy: AI may "hallucinate" or invent answers not in the docs. Tip:

Always include a strict prompt instruction ("Answer only using provided documents") 
and show the source doc to the user for verification. Test with docs that have clear, 
factual answers first. 
• Embedding/search latency: Vector databases can be overkill for small doc sets. Tip:

Start with simple full-text search; if MVP works, upgrade to vector search. For <50 
documents, string search is fast enough. 
• Role-based checklist generation: Hard to know what tasks matter for each role without 
predefined templates. Tip: Pre-create simple JSON templates for 2–3 common roles

(Engineer, Designer, Sales); let AI fill in role-specific details. Don't try to auto-generate 
entirely from docs on day 1. 
• Escalation threshold tuning: Hard to know when to escalate vs. attempt an answer. Tip: 
Start with a heuristic (if the AI response has low confidence or the question contains

keywords like "salary," "hire date," "bonus," auto-escalate). Iterate based on test runs. 
9. What a Good Demo Looks Like 
Judge watches an admin quickly upload a PDF onboarding guide and a policy doc via a clean 
interface. A "new hire" then joins the chat, selects "Engineer" as their role, and the system auto-

generates a personalized checklist (GitHub setup, team standup, code review training). The new 
hire asks "Where's the office and what's the wifi password?" and the AI responds with the right 
answer from the uploaded guide, citing the source. When they ask "What's my salary?" the 
system flags it as needing HR review and shows up in the admin escalation queue. The admin

dashboard shows the most common questions (e.g., "wifi password" asked 3 times) so leadership 
knows to add that to the FAQ. The team demos the full flow in under 2 minutes.
